cues.text: The Umayyad Advance into Gaul
By 732 Muslim forces of the Umayyad Caliphate had controlled most of the Iberian Peninsula for two decades and had begun probing north across the Pyrenees into Aquitaine.
That year Abd al-Rahman , governor of al-Andalus, led a large army across the mountains and overwhelmed Duke Eudes of Aquitaine.
He advanced deep into Frankish territory, burning and plundering as far as the Loire valley, including the wealthy monastery of Saint-Hilaire near Poitiers.
Charles Martel, Mayor of the Palace
Real power in the Frankish kingdom lay not with its Merovingian kings but with Charles Martel , illegitimate son of Pepin of Herstal.
Mayor of the Palace since 714, he had spent the previous decade consolidating Frankish unity through relentless campaigning against Frisians, Saxons, and rival Frankish nobles.
Eudes, defeated and desperate, appealed to Charles for aid despite earlier friction between them.
The Battle Between Tours and Poitiers
In October 732, Charles met the invading army somewhere between Tours and Poitiers with a largely infantry force of seasoned veterans.
According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, the two armies faced each other for several days before the decisive engagement.
In that battle, the Frankish line held firm against repeated Umayyad cavalry charges.
Abd al-Rahman was killed in the fighting, and his army, in disarray, withdrew southward overnight.
'The Hammer'

Frankish and later chroniclers portrayed the victory in providential terms, and it was this battle, tradition holds, that earned Charles his enduring epithet Martel — 'the Hammer' — for the merciless force with which he broke the enemy line.

Modern historians debate the battle's exact scale and strategic finality, since Muslim raids into southern Gaul continued for years afterward, but contemporaries and near-contemporaries alike regarded it as a turning point.
Consolidating a Christian Frontier

The victory strengthened Charles's authority immeasurably, allowing him to complete the political unification of the Frankish realms and to extend Frankish influence into Aquitaine, Burgundy, and Provence over the following decade.
His success also laid crucial groundwork for the Carolingian dynasty his son Pepin the Short would found in 751, and for his grandson Charlemagne's later imperial coronation in Rome.
Legacy
For generations of Western historians, from Gibbon onward, Tours (often called Poitiers) marked the high-water mark of the Islamic advance into Western Europe.
In the words of the Catholic Encyclopedia, it was a battle upon whose outcome depended "whether Christian Civilization should continue or Islam prevail throughout Europe."
Whatever its precise strategic weight, the battle secured Francia as the emerging center of Latin Christendom for centuries that followed.
